paper.title: Agnostic Language Identification and Generation
paper.summary: Establishes statistical rates for weak and minimal language identification and generation of an unseen word in the sampling support under agnostic IID data.

formalization_scope.summary: All nine main theorems and Corollary 3.3 of Sections 2–3 have explicit statements and proofs. A separate window-selection proof derives the sublinear-exponent upper bounds of the introduction.
specializations: Finite ordered IID samples retain multiplicities. Randomized estimators and generators are PMF-valued kernels.
Classical semantic selection expresses Algorithms 1–3. The witness index uses one ambient enumeration and zero-based word positions.
Alternative witnesses prove the existential lower bounds. The PaperMap records the distinctions for Theorems 2.3, 2.5, 3.1, and 3.4.

exclusions: Section 1 states informal summaries. Appendix proofs, examples, implementation remarks and unnumbered definitions are outside this claim inventory.

claims.title: Weak identification with an attained optimum
claims.statement_summary: For each diverging window function, the probability of returning a suboptimal language and expected excess risk along Algorithm 1 are eventually at most twice the window size times exp(−n/(2f(n)²)).

formalization.notes: An attained optimum and a diverging finite comparison window suffice.

lean_links.notes: An attained optimum and a diverging finite comparison window suffice.

audit_refs.scope: Generated declaration, module and axiom checks for Theorem 2.1.

claims.title: Exponential lower bound for weak identification
claims.statement_summary: If two distinct languages each have a private string, every randomized identifier has a distribution attaining the optimum where expected excess risk is at least exp(−5n) infinitely often.

formalization.notes: The private strings are specified extensionally, so repeated indices for the same language are allowed.

lean_links.notes: The private strings are specified extensionally, so repeated indices for the same language are allowed.

audit_refs.scope: Generated declaration, module and axiom checks for Theorem 2.2.

claims.title: Arbitrarily slow rates without an optimum
claims.statement_summary: One countable family of infinite languages works against every randomized identifier and vanishing rate R. A distribution with unattained infimum incurs excess risk at least R(n)/8 infinitely often.

formalization.notes: The finite-label averaging and Baire argument work for all real rates tending to zero.

lean_links.notes: The finite-label averaging and Baire argument work for all real rates tending to zero.

audit_refs.scope: Generated declaration, module and axiom checks for Theorem 2.3.

claims.title: Near-exponential minimal identification
claims.statement_summary: A supported tell-tale for an optimal language gives Algorithm 2 an eventual minimal-identification error bound cf(n) exp(−dn/f(n)²) for some positive c and d.

formalization.notes: The proof selects the first eligible language with a visible finite tell-tale.

lean_links.notes: The proof selects the first eligible language with a visible finite tell-tale.

audit_refs.scope: Generated declaration, module and axiom checks for Theorem 2.4.

claims.title: Minimal identification outside the supported tell-tale condition
claims.statement_summary: Every language in a fixed family admits a tell-tale, yet for each deterministic identifier a distribution with attained optimum and no optimal supported tell-tale has liminf success probability at most one half.

formalization.notes: The alternative witness has all risks zero and no inclusion-minimal optimum, as allowed by equation (4).

lean_links.notes: The alternative witness has all risks zero and no inclusion-minimal optimum, as allowed by equation (4).

claims.title: General agnostic generation obstruction
claims.statement_summary: For each positive epsilon and randomized generator a fixed infinite-support distribution has generation error at least one minus epsilon infinitely often.

formalization.notes: The universe is the natural numbers and the proof applies to every positive epsilon.

lean_links.notes: The universe is the natural numbers and the proof applies to every positive epsilon.

claims.title: Exponential generation with finite witness index
claims.statement_summary: Algorithm 3 has generation error at most c exp(−dn) under a finite witness index and a support containing one candidate language.

formalization.notes: The single ambient enumeration determines the word order in every candidate.

lean_links.notes: The single ambient enumeration determines the word order in every candidate.

audit_refs.scope: Generated declaration, module and axiom checks for Theorem 3.2.

claims.title: Exponential generation for finite language families
claims.statement_summary: A finite family of infinite languages has finite witness index. Algorithm 3 achieves exponential error decay whenever the sampling support contains a candidate.

formalization.notes: Finiteness is measured on the set of distinct languages in the indexed family.

lean_links.notes: Finiteness is measured on the set of distinct languages in the indexed family.

relations.notes: Finite collections have a finite witness index, so Theorem 3.2 applies.

claims.title: A supported language with infinite witness index
claims.statement_summary: For one fixed countable family and enumeration, each deterministic generator has a distribution containing a candidate in its support, having infinite witness index, and causing limsup error at least one half.

formalization.notes: The proof constructs a path through rows and also applies to randomized kernels.

lean_links.notes: The proof constructs a path through rows and also applies to randomized kernels.

claims.title: Exponential generation lower bound
claims.statement_summary: Two languages with finite intersection and a common outside word give, for each randomized generator, a distribution containing a candidate in its support with generation error at least exp(−2n)/4 infinitely often.

formalization.notes: The finite intersection can be nonempty and the lower bound holds for a fixed distribution.

lean_links.notes: The finite intersection can be nonempty and the lower bound holds for a fixed distribution.
